documents.abstract: Android apps handle sensitive data, often displayed on screens (i.e., Activities), and protecting these activities is vital for ensuring user privacy. Several studies have demonstrated the risk of private data leakage via screen capture and identified malware exploiting this vulnerability. To mitigate such threats, Google introduced FLAG_SECURE, an activity-level security feature that protects an Activity when set by blocking screen capture and restricting display on non-secure devices. Proper usage of this security feature could significantly reduce data leakage risks. However, to the best of our knowledge, its adoption across diverse Android apps has not been systematically studied. In this work, we present a large-scale empirical study of screenshot-based vulnerabilities in Android apps using a systematic static analysis pipeline, ASSA. The pipeline automatically constructs UI models of activities and fragments by leveraging a customized version of Frontmatter, and combines them with a Large Language Model (LLM) to infer runtime context and identify sensitive user data rendered on screens. We apply ASSA to 5,667 popular real-world Android apps and find that 19.8% contain at least one activity that displays sensitive information without screen-capture protection, while 87.2% of apps do not apply FLAG_SECURE to any activity, exposing credentials, financial information, and location data to screenshot attacks. Beyond quantifying prevalence, we analyze FLAG_SECURE usage patterns and establish a taxonomy that captures diverse factors influencing developers’ decisions to adopt or omit screen protection, including intentional privacy protection, intellectual property safeguarding, and unintentional inheritance from base activities. To assess real-world impact, we further conduct in-depth case studies on 200 vulnerable apps and responsibly disclose our findings to the affected vendors, receiving 6 confirmed patches and 20 acknowledgments, including 11 vendors who reported ongoing efforts toward mitigation. These findings indicate that screenshot-based vulnerabilities are not only widespread but also systematically overlooked in practice, highlighting the need for greater awareness and more careful handling of sensitive on-screen information by developers.

Background Patients recovering from lumbar fusion increasingly seek guidance from large language model (LLM) chatbots when their surgeon is unavailable, but the accuracy, completeness, and safety-related content of such responses have not been compared across models for the postoperative period. Objective To compare the accuracy, quality, safety-related content, and readability of responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude to frequently asked postoperative lumbar fusion questions, and to identify the question types for which responses are weakest. Methods Thirty questions, compiled by three neurosurgeons and grouped into six clinical categories, were submitted to each model, each with a standardized, patient-oriented prompt requesting warning signs. Ninety anonymized, randomized responses were rated independently by three blinded neurosurgeons for accuracy and four quality subdomains (clarity, completeness, relevance, and patient safety) on 4-point scales. Readability (Flesch–Kincaid, Flesch Reading Ease, and Gunning Fog), word count, and responses meeting an operational screening criterion for potential harm were also assessed. Models were compared with Friedman and Holm-corrected pairwise tests. Results Accuracy was high for all models without significant differences. Quality, clarity, completeness, relevance, and patient safety differed globally, but effect sizes were small (Kendall's W : 0.10–0.21) and, after correction across the six outcome families, only quality and completeness remained significant, with Gemini scoring lower than ChatGPT and Claude. Gemini had the most favorable readability. ChatGPT responses were the shortest (mean 294 vs. 462 and 445 words); length was unrelated to completeness or readability. Two Gemini responses (6.7%) and none from ChatGPT or Claude met a post hoc operational screening criterion for potential harm (a score of ≤2 on accuracy or patient safety from at least one of three raters, without concurrence from the other two); no response was adjudicated as actually harmful. In exploratory question- and category-level analyses, responses tended to be rated highest for standardized questions and lowest for those requiring individualized judgment or interpretation of wound-related symptoms. Conclusion Responses from contemporary LLMs to common postoperative lumbar fusion questions were generally rated as accurate, with small between-model differences and a model-level divergence between readability and completeness. Because safety-related content was explicitly prompted and no patient outcomes were assessed, these findings describe the quality of safety-related information rather than clinical safety. LLMs may support postoperative patient education but should not replace physician guidance, particularly for warning signs and patient-specific recovery decisions.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Low back pain (LBP) is one of the most common musculoskeletal disorders among office workers due to prolonged sitting, continuous computer use, and poor ergonomic posture. Age and length of employment are factors suspected to contribute to LBP complaints because they are associated with degenerative changes in the musculoskeletal system and cumulative exposure to occupational risk factors. Methods: This study employed an analytical observational design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of all employees of the Department of Culture and Tourism and the Department of Communication and Informatics of Batam City Government who met the study criteria. A total of 86 respondents were selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were analyzed using the Chi-Square test with a significance level of p<0.05. Results: Statistical analysis showed a significant relationship between age and Low Back Pain complaints (p=0.019) and a significant relationship between length of employment and Low Back Pain complaints (p<0.001). Conclusion: There was a significant relationship between age and length of employment and Low back pain complaints among employees of the Department of Culture and Tourism and the Department of Communication and Informatics of Batam City Government Keywords: Age, Length of Employment, Low back pain.

This chapter examines the evidence base for human and organizational factors (HOF) as an approach to managing OSH, critically evaluating its theoretical coherence, its practical distinctiveness, and its field-validated impact on injury reduction. It describes HOF as an eclectic, sociotechnical integrative domain drawing from industrial, occupational, organizational psychology, ergonomics, and sociology, while noting that it lacks unique practical interventions and operates primarily as a knowledge broker rather than a distinct scientific discipline. The chapter highlights HOF&s;s reliance on non-falsifiable, post-hoc interpretive frameworks, and its problematic dismissal of human error as a valid root cause in incident investigations. Drawing on the available field studies across human factors engineering, ergonomics, human performance improvement, and sociological approaches to safety, it provides practitioners with a critical evidence-based appraisal of HOF, concluding that its claimed contributions to OSH exceed what the field-validated evidence currently supports.

The main objective of this study is to explore how pre-service teachers retrospectively describe differences between their prior and current perspectives following participation in a Human Library. This research begins with a review of the literature on the definition and characteristics of Human Libraries and proceeds with the creation of one in a university setting. To this end, the study benefited from the collaboration of the Baketik Foundation, which facilitated contact with five individuals willing to share their testimonies on topics related to human rights. The initial sample consisted of 53 pre-service teachers in the Early Childhood Education Bachelor’s programme at the University of the Basque Country (EHU), although ultimately, following a screening process, the sample was reduced to 51. Data were collected using the “I used to think…/Now I think…” reflection exercise, which the pre-service teachers were asked to complete after listening to the testimonies. The narratives were first examined manually by the researchers to identify recurring ideas and potential thematic categories. Microsoft Copilot and ChatGPT were subsequently used to support the identification and consistency checking of the initial category structure, while the final coding was conducted manually by the researchers. Six thematic categories were identified in both sections of the reflection exercise. The descriptive comparison revealed differences in the frequency and elaboration of participants’ narratives, particularly regarding empathy and changes in perspective, peace and social justice, women’s rights and gender-based violence, and silence, social taboos and lack of awareness. Because both sections were produced retrospectively after the Human Library experience, these differences are interpreted as features of participants’ accounts rather than as direct evidence of objectively measured changes in their perspectives.

documents.abstract: Introduction The transition to Industry 5.0 is transforming manufacturing through the integration of smart technologies, while simultaneously increasing the need to protect workers’ health and reduce occupational risks. This systematic review synthesized cross-sectoral evidence on human-centered Industry 5.0 technologies for assessing and reducing occupational risks, with a focus on ergonomic outcomes, worker-related factors, and the conditions influencing their implementation and transferability. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science following the PRISMA 2020 framework and predefined eligibility criteria based on PECO. Included studies were analyzed according to technology type, occupational risk addressed, ergonomic dimension, assessment method, reported outcomes, implementation conditions, and implications for occupational health and safety, yielding a total of 78 studies that met the inclusion criteria. Results The reported results from individual studies included ergonomic assessment accuracies exceeding 95%, fatigue reductions of more than 50% in selected applications, and cycle-time reductions of up to 28.4%, along with improvements in task allocation, workload monitoring, and production efficiency. These values should not be interpreted as overall effects of Industry 5.0 technologies, given the heterogeneity of technologies, experimental designs, and assessment methods. Discussion The evidence was limited by laboratory validation, a lack of longitudinal research, heterogeneous assessment methods, and insufficient real-world implementation in specific industrial sectors.

Industry 5.0 (I5.0) emphasizes industrial technologies that are human-centric, sustainable, and resilient. Human-Centric Digital Twins (HCDTs) support this transition by integrating worker data with robots, machines, tasks, and industrial environments. However, the relevant research remains fragmented across human modelling, Human–Robot Collaboration, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation, and Digital Twin (DT) research. Moreover, systems that use human data or adaptive automation are often described as human-centric without demonstrating measurable benefits to workers. This review addresses these limitations by distinguishing HCDTs from conventional human models, Human DTs, and collaborative robotic systems. It critically examines human-focused sensing, multi-modal data integration, biomechanical modelling, intention and motion prediction, robotic simulation, optimization, reinforcement learning, immersive interfaces, industrial connectivity, and data governance. Based on this analysis, a literature-derived conceptual framework is proposed that connects sensing, integration, human modelling, analytics, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, human interaction, and governance. The framework organizes the functional requirements of HCDTs and is intended to inform future system design and comparison; its practical applicability and effectiveness require further validation. The review argues that HCDTs must extend beyond worker monitoring and productivity maximization: human data should inform industrial decisions that produce measurable improvements in safety, ergonomics, wellbeing, autonomy, accessibility, or skill development. Such systems should also uphold privacy, transparency, uncertainty awareness, explainability, and appropriate human authority. By linking technological capabilities to explicit worker outcomes, this synthesis enables researchers and engineers to assess the human-centeredness of HCDT implementations and supports the development of trustworthy systems for I5.0.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in land governance, reshaping how environmental pressures and sustainability goals are addressed. Yet the institutional processes through which human–AI collaboration takes shape remain largely unexplored. This study examines whether human–AI collaboration is emerging as a new governance paradigm in China’s land sector, and if so, through what institutional pathways and practical forms it is being articulated and implemented. Drawing on a systematic analysis of 352 policy documents and case studies from coastal regions, the study develops and applies the CTI framework—an analytical lens that integrates Contextual conditions, Technological capabilities, and Institutional arrangements. The findings reveal three interrelated developments: (1) policy discourse constructs a coherent narrative in which environmental pressures and digital transformation jointly create an imperative for change; (2) a systematic division of labor between AI and human officials emerges in policy and is reflected in practice, with AI handling data processing and preliminary screening while humans retain final decision-making, value judgment, and accountability; and (3) this division is being institutionalized through a staged process of policy guidance, pilot mechanisms, and institutional adaptation. These developments suggest that human–AI collaboration may be taking shape as an emerging governance paradigm in land governance, one that is beginning to be codified and tested in policy and practice. The study contributes an integrative analytical framework, specifies the logic of human–machine division of labor, and extends collaborative governance theory beyond its traditional human-centric assumptions. The findings also carry implications for governance contexts where human–AI collaboration is reshaping land governance and other policy domains.

documents.abstract: Abstract This research involved co-creating a systematic review analysis alongside the world’s smartest humanoid robot, Ami. The work involved a human-humanoid collaboration in understanding driving under the influence of drugs’ (DUIDs’) prevalence, implications and chemical analysis. The systematic review was conducted according to the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis guidelines. Quantitative studies reporting drugs encountered in DUID published between 2007 – 2025 were included. Studies that had no confirmatory chemical analysis were excluded. Included studies ( n = 25) were analysed independently by researchers and integrated into Ami’s knowledge-based system. Ami deployed large language models for analysis but often needed prompt to extract information. The results showed similarity in extraction between the systematic review and the humanoid analysis. Both approaches confirmed key drugs reported in DUID were alcohol, cannabinoids, cocaine, amphetamine, benzodiazepines, and opiates. Such drugs were often detected in blood and urine and less occasionally in oral fluid. Key techniques employed for their analysis were immunoassay, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, where the latter was the most sensitive technique. Implications of these drugs on driving included impairment, increased risk of accidents, with fatal accidents less frequent but more severe. No AI hallucinations were encountered in Ami’s answers; yet, examples were used from outside the studies integrated into the knowledge-based system. This showed that the humanoid is integrating experience and knowledge from other sourcing and adapting them in the present study. In summary, the humanoid offered a valuable and quick tool in analysis and can support healthcare research.

As the dimensionality and complexity of engineering data grows, traditional machine learning systems become increasinglydifficult to apply, especially when detecting informative features without sacrificing predictive accuracy and computationalefficiency. In this paper we proposed a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning Framework for Intelligent Feature Optimization andPredictive Analytics in Engineering Applications. The framework is a combination of classical data preprocessing, intelligentfeature selection, quantum-enhanced feature representation, parameterized quantum circuits and predictive learning in a unifiedoptimization pipeline. Engineering features are first normalized and evaluated to find informative subsets and minimizeredundancy. These selected features are then mapped onto the quantum feature space and parameterized quantum circuits tocreate improved representations for predictive modeling. The optimization objective takes into account predictive loss, size ofthe feature subset and regularization to achieve an efficient feature configuration. This quantum-classical representation is fed to the classical predictive models for classification and evaluation of the models. The framework is assessed based on predictiveaccuracy, ROC properties, feature reduction, convergence behavior, computational time, scalability and prediction error. Thepotential of using intelligent feature optimization combined with quantum enhanced representation for engineering analytics isillustrated by comparing it to conventional machine learning and hybrid learning models. This study provides a flexibleframework that enables the merging of quantum and classic machine learning, and shows how hybrid architectures can be usedin high-dimensional engineering prediction.

Background: Brain tumor surgery aims to achieve maximal safe resection while preserving neurological function; however, accurate intraoperative discrimination between tumor tissue and normal brain remains a major challenge. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has emerged as a promising label-free optical imaging modality that provides quantitative information on tissue biochemical and physiological characteristics. The integration of machine learning (ML) has further enhanced its potential for automated tissue classification and real-time intraoperative decision support. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding HSI and ML in brain tumor surgery, highlighting technological principles, clinical applications, current limitations, and future directions. Methods: This narrative review was based on a comprehensive literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify studies evaluating the application of HSI and artificial intelligence (AI) in brain tumor surgery. The search strategy included combinations of the keywords “ hyperspectral imaging ,” “ brain tumor ,” “ glioma ,” “ machine learning ,” “ deep learning ,” “ artificial intelligence ,” and “ neurosurgery .” Priority was given to peer-reviewed original research articles, narrative and systematic reviews, and clinically relevant investigations describing the technical development, intraoperative application, and translational potential of HSI in neurooncology. Landmark studies that established the foundations of HSI, together with recent publications reflecting advances in ML and clinical implementation, were preferentially included to provide both historical context and contemporary perspectives. Manual screening of the reference lists of key publications was performed to identify additional relevant studies. As a narrative review, this manuscript was intended to provide a critical overview of current evidence rather than a systematic assessment of the literature. Consequently, no formal study selection algorithm, quality assessment tool, or quantitative meta-analysis was performed. Results: Current evidence indicates that HSI combined with ML enables accurate intraoperative tissue classification, improved tumor margin delineation, and emerging molecular characterization, including prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation status. Deep learning approaches generally outperform conventional ML techniques by integrating spectral and spatial information. Although early clinical studies have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance, widespread implementation remains limited by heterogeneous imaging protocols, relatively small patient cohorts, limited multicenter validation, and computational challenges. Conclusion: HSI represents a promising adjunct for precision-guided brain tumor surgery by providing real-time biochemical tissue characterization without the need for exogenous contrast agents. Continued advances in AI, standardized imaging protocols, multicenter clinical validation, and multimodal intraoperative integration will be essential to facilitate routine clinical adoption and establish its impact on surgical and patient outcomes.

I·V·O Lens Prompt v4.1 is the current canonical reference version of the I·V·O Lens, a domain-independent framework for structural analysis using: O — Structured PossibilityV — Instantiated RelationI — Situated Selectivity Version 4.1 retains the operator semantics frozen in v4.0 and introduces additional epistemic safeguards developed from reproducible cross-model failure modes. The v4.1 safeguards strengthen: evidence provenance and claim-status separation; distinction between observation, event, class, membership and mechanism; separation of hypothesized mechanisms from established structural conditions; treatment of UNRESOLVED versus supported negative claims; evidential dependency and uncertainty propagation; causal-status calibration; requirements for assigning Situated Selectivity (I); synthesis and intervention constraints. The release candidate underlying v4.1 was frozen and tested in a controlled cross-model Hessdalen regression using Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. The regression substantially reduced the targeted failure modes without collapsing the analysis into blanket uncertainty. The exact tested RC2 artefact is retained in the release archive for reproducibility. This Zenodo release includes the canonical v4.1 prompt as a directly accessible file, release notes, a cross-model Hessdalen regression note, citation metadata, checksums, licensing information, and a complete public archive. The digital revolution is transforming modern education as it moves from teacher lecture to learner-centered, interactive methods. Immersive technologies augment learning using Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Extended Reality (XR) in conjunction with the use of multimedia to enable experiential and collaborative learning. This chapter gives a review of concepts, pedagogical foundations, applications and implementation of immersive technology in various educational fields. It also explores the effectiveness of learning, the implementation challenges, ethical issues, and future trends like Metaverse education, adaptive XR and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Moreover, the chapter reviews the recent literature and outlines the gaps in the current research to offer practical implications for the educators, instructional designers, and researchers.

Background Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous whole-joint disorder influenced by mechanical stress, aging, previous trauma, genetic susceptibility, subchonrral bone alterations, and localized inflamation.Emerging evidence suggests that immune and metabolic processes alterations may be involved in OA pathogenesis particularly in inflammatory and metabolically dysregulated subtypes. Content This narrative review summarizes the bidirectional crosstalk between immune and metabolic processes during OA progression. Human observational studies and experimental models suggest that immune-cell activation and metabolic dysfunction may interact to influence synovial inflammation and cartilage homeostasis although their causal relevance and relative contributions vary across OA phenotypes. We further discuss emerging immunometabolic strategies targeting glycolytic and lipid-metabolic pathways as well as predominantly experimental approaches involving gene editing synthetic biology and stem cell-based therapies. Conclusion Integrating multi-omics technologies with personalized medicine may improve patient stratification and dynamic monitoring and could facilitate the future development of more personalized and potentially disease-modifying strategies for OA.Future research should focus on clarifying the dynamic immunometabolic network underlying OA and promoting the clinical translation of innovative strategies through artificial intelligence and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Human resource management (HRM) is being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI). Organisations increasingly use AI to screen applicants, schedule interviews, personalise learning, provide continuous performance feedback, predict attrition, answer employee queries and allocate work. These AI-enabled HR practices promise efficiency, consistency and personalisation, but they also alter the relationship between employees and the organisation in ways that shape attitudes, behaviours and performance. This chapter examines the impact of AI-enabled HR practices on organisational behaviour and employee performance. It first clarifies the concepts of electronic HRM, HR analytics, algorithmic HRM and AI-enabled HRM and traces their evolution. It then reviews AI applications across the HR value chain, from workforce planning and recruitment to learning, performance management, compensation, engagement, retention and HR service delivery. Drawing on the ability–motivation–opportunity framework, social exchange theory, organisational justice theory, the job demands–resources model, psychological contract theory and technology acceptance theories, the chapter explains the mechanisms through which AI-enabled HR practices influence trust, perceived fairness, engagement, job satisfaction, autonomy, technostress, job insecurity and, ultimately, task, contextual and innovative performance. A synthesis of empirical evidence shows that effects are contingent: AI-enabled HR practices tend to improve outcomes when they are transparent, fair, augmentative and supported by leadership, and to undermine them when they are opaque, controlling or perceived as reductive. The chapter proposes an integrative conceptual framework with research propositions, discusses ethical and legal considerations, including India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and offers practical guidance for managers.

documents.abstract: Astronomy and space are undergoing a transformation in how they are explored and understood by human visitors, thanks to technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), satellite imaging, mobile applications, smart telescopes, and astrophotography devices. Mobile Sky Mapping Applications allow visitors to find planets, stars, and constellations in real time. Weather predictions, visibility updates, and customized tips for optimal viewing conditions are all possible with AI systems. Similarly, AR and VR technologies can offer a virtual experience by generating simulated space and astronomical phenomena, enabling tourists to virtually travel through space to explore galaxies and planets that would be impossible to reach in the real world. Telescopes have become more accessible to amateur astronomers and tourists, thanks to new telescope technology and automated observatories. Satellite technology is utilized to help determine areas with dark skies and reduced light pollution. These technologies enhance tourists’ engagement and learning, raise scientific awareness, help protect the environment, and boost economic opportunities for tourism areas in remote regions. The results of this study point to the potential of different technologies to transform astro tourism and offer new, educational, and immersive experiences worldwide.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly available to students, but their educational value depends on how they are configured, constrained, and integrated into course practices. This technology report describes a no-code workflow for implementing a course-specific chatbot in upper-division undergraduate biochemistry using a custom GPT configured with instructor-generated lecture slides, class transcripts, handouts, syllabus information, and custom instructions. The workflow emphasized course alignment, frequent updating, instructor validation, assessment scoping, and student prompt guidance. The chatbot was used in biochemistry I lecture across two consecutive fall offerings and extended to biochemistry II lecture for follow-up use. Student survey responses indicated substantial adoption and generally positive perceptions; peer-led supplemental instruction attendance and course-grade data are presented only as contextual information. The report highlights a practical, transferable approach for using no-code custom GPT tools to extend course-aligned study support while preserving instructor oversight and existing academic support structures.

documents.abstract: Uzbekistan has moved further and faster on small-business reform than most countries in the post-Soviet region. Between 2017 and 2025 the share of small business in GDP rose from roughly one third to over half, and the number of registered small entities reached 1.21 million by October 2025 (State Statistics Agency, 2025). The country was recognised as one of the five largest global improvers in the 2024 Women, Business and the Law index, with an 11.9-point gain taking its score to 82.5 (World Bank, 2024). The Uzbekistan-2030 strategy targets a doubling of exports and an increase in the number of exporting enterprises from roughly 5,700 to 15,000 (Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, 2024).These figures have been read almost exclusively through an economic and engineering lens. The dominant policy frame treats market infrastructure as a matter of roads, customs procedures, payment systems, credit lines and digital platforms. That frame is not wrong. It is incomplete in a specific and consequential way, and the way it is incomplete is sociological. This article makes a conceptual argument rather than reporting new data. Our contribution is not the observation that markets are socially embedded, which has been established since Polanyi (1944) and Granovetter (1985). It is threefold and more specific.First, we argue that the social layer of market infrastructure should be treated as infrastructure in its own right, not as context surrounding the "real" infrastructure. This extends to a post-Soviet setting the argument developed by Elyachar (2010) for Cairo, where the communicative channels produced by women's everyday sociality function as economic infrastructure in the same register as roads and telephone lines, and it connects that argument to Star's (1999) and Larkin's (2013) insistence that infrastructure is relational and becomes visible only through the practices that sustain or fail to sustain it.Second, we specify the mechanism by which social structure acts on formally universal infrastructure. We call it differential access filtering, and we decompose it using the four sources of social capital distinguished by Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993), namely value introjection, bounded solidarity, reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust. Two of these enable market participation and two constrain it, which gives the framework an internal reason to expect both positive and negative effects rather than asserting one or the other.Third, we propose Uzbekistan as a scope condition for embeddedness theory. Most of the informality and embeddedness literature has examined settings where formal institutions were weak, absent or decaying (Mair and Martí, 2009;Williams and Shahid, 2016). Uzbekistan presents the inverse configuration, in which formal market infrastructure is being built rapidly and from above onto a dense, legally codified communal institution. The theoretical question this raises is whether embeddedness under rapid state-led formalisation produces bridging or closure, and our answer is that it systematically produces both, with the balance determined by which of the four mechanisms a given reform activates.The article proceeds as follows. Section 2 develops the theoretical framing. Section 3 sets out the fivelayer framework and its social mediators. Section 4 reads the mahalla symmetrically. Section 5 applies the framework differentially to five entrepreneurial positions. Section 6 states explicitly what the available evidence does and does not support. Section 7 discusses feasibility of the policy implications. Section 8 sets out the theoretical contribution, limitations, testable propositions and research agenda.Infrastructure studies in sociology and anthropology have moved decisively away from treating infrastructure as a stock of physical assets. Star (1999) argued that infrastructure is relational rather than substantive, that it is embedded in other structures and practices, and that its distributional properties become visible mainly at the point of breakdown. Larkin (2013) extended this by treating infrastructures as objects that carry political and aesthetic meaning as well as goods, and by showing that the promise attached to an infrastructure is part of what it does. Graham and Marvin (2001) documented the process by which networked infrastructure, far from producing uniform access, splinters into premium and residual circuits. Elyachar (2010) took the argument one step further in a way that is directly relevant here. Studying microfinance and empowerment projects in Cairo, she showed that the communicative channels generated by women's routine sociality constitute a social infrastructure that carries economic traffic as surely as a road does, and that development interventions make this infrastructure visible precisely by attempting to capture or format it. We take this as our starting point. If social ties are infrastructure, then a five-layer account of market infrastructure is not a four-layer account plus context. It is an account of five infrastructures, one of which happens to be made of relationships.Economic sociology supplies the mechanism. Granovetter (1985) established that economic action is embedded in concrete networks of relations. Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993) then did the analytical work that the embeddedness literature most often omits, distinguishing four mechanisms by which social structure shapes economic action and, crucially, identifying their positive and negative consequences together. Value introjection and bounded solidarity generate commitment and mutual support but also generate demands for conformity. Reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust lower transaction costs but also impose obligations that can drain the successful and restrict the individual autonomy on which enterprise growth depends. Portes and Landolt (1996) and Portes (1998) developed the resulting downsides, namely exclusion of outsiders, excess claims on group members, restrictions on individual freedom and downward levelling norms. We adopt this four-mechanism decomposition as the analytical core of our framework, because it is what allows a symmetrical reading of communal institutions rather than a celebratory one.Two further strands complete the framing. The contextualisation programme in entrepreneurship research insists that where and when entrepreneurship happens is constitutive rather than incidental (Welter, 2011;Welter et al., 2019), and Kloosterman's (2010) mixed embeddedness perspective shows how the resources an entrepreneur can mobilise from social networks interact with the opportunity structure that markets and regulation supply. Meanwhile, the entrepreneurial ecosystem literature has become the dominant policy vocabulary for the phenomena we describe, and its own systematic reviews concede that it remains largely atheoretical and built on advanced-economy assumptions, with resource scarcity, structural gaps and institutional voids distinguishing emergingeconomy ecosystems (Cao and Shi, 2021;Wurth et al., 2022). Our framework is intended in part as a sociological supplement to that literature, replacing its metaphor of an ecosystem of actors with an account of layered infrastructures and the filters that regulate access to them.By market infrastructure we mean the bundle of arrangements that allow a small firm to find customers, set prices, secure finance, manage logistics and enforce rights. We distinguish five layers. The physical layer covers roads, warehouses, bazaars and border posts. The financial layer covers banks, microfinance, payment instruments and credit lines. The digital layer covers e-commerce, platform identifiers, e-government and data systems (Nambisan, 2017;Bonina et al., 2021). The institutional layer covers registration, taxation, standards and dispute resolution. The social layer covers trust networks, reputational systems, professional associations, rotating savings groups and the mahalla.The analytically important claim is not the existence of five layers but the relation between them. Access to any of the first four layers is mediated through the fifth, and the fifth distributes that access unequally. A credit assessment reads a reputation that is produced in a network. A customs procedure is navigated with the help of brokers and peers who have navigated it before. A digital marketplace is adopted first by entrepreneurs whose existing ties already include early users, which is why platform adoption tends to follow pre-existing network structure rather than to disrupt it (Bonina et al., 2021).Where public investment addresses the first four layers without engaging the fifth, returns are eroded by filtering rather than by underprovision. The new road serves the bazaar of the better connected. The new credit line reaches firms with formal collateral. The new platform recruits younger urban men with smartphones and foreign-language skills. This is the splintering dynamic that Graham and Marvin (2001) described, produced here by social rather than commercial sorting.Urban evidence from Uzbekistan supports this reading at the level of the layers themselves. Farmanov et al. (2025), examining smart-city implementation in Bukhara, find that deployment of sensors, platforms and digital governance tools has run ahead of the inclusivity and citizen-engagement components, so that a technically advancing infrastructure is not correspondingly more usable. Dushanova et al. (2025) document the same asymmetry in the city's tourism infrastructure, where heritage sites, transport and wayfinding remain inaccessible to people with mobility impairments despite a national policy commitment to barrier-free provision. Both cases show a filter that is not social in the network sense but produces the same result, namely infrastructure that is formally universal and practically selective. They also support treating market infrastructure as a sociotechnical assembly rather than a technical one, which is the premise of Section 2.In the Uzbek case we identify five social mediators through which the filtering runs, namely mahalla networks, gender norms and the unpaid care burden, the urban-rural divide, the informal economy, and labour migration. These are not causes in a statistical sense and we do not claim to have estimated their effects. They are the channels through which formally universal infrastructure becomes differentially accessible, and Section 6 states precisely how much evidence stands behind each.Figure 1. Five-layer framework of market infrastructure for small entrepreneurship in Uzbekistan. Infrastructure layers reach policy outcomes only through social mediators. Each mediator has an enabling and a restricting side, corresponding to the four mechanisms of social capital in Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993). Which side dominates depends on the mechanism a given reform activates.mahalla solidarity has historically rested on residence rather than kinship or ethnicity, which gave it an unusually broad reach across social groups. Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) describe the mahalla as a legally plural arena in which competing orders coexist and produce new organisational forms, some of them generative.On the restricting side, the record is at least as substantial and considerably older than our earlier draft acknowledged. Three findings matter for market infrastructure specifically.First, the mahalla's incorporation into public administration has converted an association of residents into an instrument of state administration and, in the assessment of a large body of work, of social control (Urinboyev, 2011;Noori, 2006;Human Rights Watch, 2003). Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) situate this within broader debates on how non-democratic states neutralise civil-society institutions through administrative and legal incorporation. An entrepreneur's relationship with the mahalla is therefore not a purely horizontal relationship among peers. It carries a vertical dimension, and any policy that routes market infrastructure through the mahalla routes it through that vertical dimension too.Second, mahalla-based discretionary allocation has documented exclusionary effects along gender lines. Kamp (2004) shows that the delegation of welfare targeting to mahalla committees, staffed by untrained neighbours exercising discretion, placed divorced and abandoned women at particular risk of exclusion, and that solidarity among women in a mahalla cannot be assumed. This is bounded solidarity and enforceable trust operating exactly as Portes and Sensenbrenner predicted, producing support for insiders and exclusion at the boundary. If discretionary neighbourhood assessment produces this pattern in welfare, there is no principled reason to expect a different pattern when the same bodies certify cooperatives, endorse borrowers or vouch for exporters.Third, the conformity costs fall unevenly. Restrictions on individual autonomy and downward levelling norms are the two downsides of social capital most directly relevant to enterprise growth (Portes, 1998;Portes and Landolt, 1996). Ethnographic work on women traders in Uzbek bazaars describes exactly this tension, with women negotiating and renegotiating patriarchal norms rather than simply being enabled or simply being blocked by them (Kandiyoti, 2007).The implication for policy is that "recognise the mahalla" is an underspecified instruction. What matters is which mechanism a given reform activates. Instruments that work through reciprocity exchange, such as linking gap groups to formal microfinance, plausibly extend access. Instruments that work through discretionary gatekeeping, such as making mahalla endorsement a condition of registration, credit or certification, plausibly reproduce existing exclusions and add a vertical dependency. Three points follow from the table. The binding constraint differs by position, so a single infrastructure package cannot be expected to have uniform effects. The same mechanism that helps one position hinders another, which is why a framework built on Portes and Sensenbrenner's symmetric account is more useful here than one built on social capital as an unambiguous good. The goal of program synthesis is to enable non-expert users to write programs by providing a specification instead of an implementation. To truly realize this goal, the specification must require no expertise and no effort to generate. We consider the problem of synthesizing automation scripts from only the logs that are automatically collected by many systems. Using our approach, users can automate tasks they usually perform manually, without having to know how to program them. Because logs are collected automatically, the synthesis approach needs to scale to large sets of logs. We present a new algorithm to solve this task by incrementally extending an API-calling script with behavior exemplified by a sequence of log events, adding one sequence at a time. By minimizing the program modifications at each step, we preserve user intent and synthesize a program as general as possible. We show that our approach, implemented in a tool LogLoom, scales to synthesis tasks with more traces and more complex programs than existing techniques. LogLoom synthesizes scripts that are identical to reference solutions for 60 out of 72 benchmarks, compared to 14 for an existing symbolic approach and 39 for an LLM.

Innovative process reengineering techniques are essential for financial institutions seeking to maximize efficiency and adapt to rapidly evolving market dynamics. This Review explores the key concepts and strategies involved in implementing such techniques. Financial institutions are constantly under pressure to enhance efficiency, reduce costs, and improve customer satisfaction. To achieve these goals, many institutions are turning to innovative process reengineering techniques. These techniques involve rethinking and redesigning existing processes to streamline operations, eliminate redundancies, and improve overall efficiency. One of the key concepts in innovative process reengineering is the use of technology to automate manual tasks and improve workflow efficiency. For example, robotic process automation (RPA) can be used to automate repetitive tasks, such as data entry and reconciliation, freeing up employees to focus on more value-added activities. Similarly, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can be used to analyze large volumes of data and generate insights that can inform decision-making and improve operational efficiency. Another important aspect of innovative process reengineering is the use of data analytics to identify inefficiencies and opportunities for improvement. By analyzing data from various sources, financial institutions can gain valuable insights into their operations and identify areas where processes can be streamlined or optimized. For example, data analytics can be used to identify bottlenecks in the loan approval process or inefficiencies in the customer onboarding process, allowing institutions to make targeted improvements. In addition to technology and data analytics, innovative process reengineering techniques also involve rethinking organizational structures and culture. Financial institutions need to foster a culture of continuous improvement and innovation, where employees are encouraged to identify and implement process improvements. This may involve changing the way teams are organized, promoting collaboration across departments, and empowering employees to take ownership of process improvement initiatives. Overall, innovative process reengineering techniques are essential for financial institutions looking to maximize efficiency and stay competitive in today's rapidly changing business environment. By embracing technology, data analytics, and a culture of innovation, financial institutions can streamline their operations, reduce costs, and improve customer satisfaction.

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to understand problems from multiple perspectives. In the define stage, students formulated problems more systematically by identifying causal relationships and the underlying social contexts. The ideate stage encouraged students to generate alternative solutions creatively and collaboratively through group discussions and AI-supported idea development. In the prototype and test stages, students developed solution designs in the form of programmes or simple policy models and evaluated their effectiveness through reflection, feedback and AI-assisted analysis. The study concludes that AI supports, but does not replace, students’ critical reasoning, the quality of which depends on reflective pedagogical design.

The rapid evolution of decentralized finance (DeFi) has ushered in transformative opportunities for global financial inclusion, digital asset management, and permissionless transactions. However, the growth of DeFi also presents significant challenges related to data integrity, security, scalability, and regulatory compliance. This paper proposes a novel datadriven model that integrates blockchain technology with artificial intelligence (AI) to address these challenges and optimize DeFi operations. By leveraging the transparency, immutability, and decentralization of blockchain in conjunction with AI's predictive analytics, automation, and pattern recognition capabilities, this integrated framework enhances the resilience, efficiency, and scalability of DeFi systems. The model introduces an intelligent smart contract ecosystem powered by AI algorithms for fraud detection, anomaly monitoring, and automated compliance auditing. Machine learning techniques are applied to real-time transactional data across decentralized exchanges (DEXs), liquidity pools, and lending platforms to identify suspicious behaviors and mitigate risks proactively. Furthermore, the use of blockchain ensures tamper-proof audit trails, consensus-driven trust, and transparent governance, thus increasing user confidence and institutional adoption. Scalability is addressed through the application of layer-2 blockchain solutions and AI-based resource optimization strategies, enabling faster transaction throughput and reduced latency. Privacy-preserving AI models such as federated learning and homomorphic encryption are integrated to maintain user confidentiality while allowing intelligent data analysis. The paper also highlights potential use cases in automated asset management, decentralized credit scoring, and cross-chain interoperability. This interdisciplinary approach presents a secure, adaptive, and scalable paradigm for the next generation of DeFi systems. It aligns with global trends toward decentralized digital economies and offers a robust foundation for financial innovation, especially in regions with limited access to traditional banking infrastructure. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's implementation roadmap, potential limitations, and regulatory implications. The integration of blockchain with AI in DeFi offers not only technical advantages but also the potential to redefine trust, security, and efficiency in the global financial ecosystem.

Purpose: Knowledge management (KM) is recognized as a critical strategic framework that enables organizations to effectively leverage intellectual assets and enhance operational efficiency. In the water treatment industry, KM involves the collection, organization, sharing, and utilization of employees’ technical knowledge and specialized expertise. This process promotes technological innovation, increases system productivity, and improves service quality. Recently, the role of KM in organizations, including the water sector, has evolved to become closely integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). This development has garnered significant scholarly attention, leading to a growing body of research. One of the most effective methods to evaluate these research outputs is scientometric analysis. Therefore, this study examines scientific production in the field of intelligent KM in water treatment, aiming to identify thematic trends, collaboration networks, research gaps, and future research priorities.Methodology: This applied research utilizes scientometric techniques to analyze scientific publications related to intelligent knowledge management (KM) in water purification. Relevant articles were retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. From an initial pool of 172 documents, 49 were selected after screening titles, abstracts, and keywords. Scientometric analyses were performed using the bibliometrix package in R. To address the research questions, bibliometric methods and word co-occurrence networks were employed. Frequent keywords were identified, dominant conceptual clusters were mapped, and influential thematic trends were examined. Additionally, strategic diagrams, thematic mapping, and hierarchical clustering were used to construct a comprehensive science map of the field.Findings: Since 2015, there has been an increasing focus on knowledge management in this field. In 2024, the highest number of documents was published, totaling eight scientific productions. Other notable years include 2022 and 2018, with seven and five articles published, respectively, demonstrating a growing trend. China, the United States, and the United Kingdom were the most active countries, contributing 11, 10, and 6 scientific documents, respectively. Beijing University of Technology and Tianjin University have played crucial roles in generating knowledge and advancing new technologies in this area. The journal IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics, with three articles, ranks first among sources publishing documents, with most sources classified as Q1. The top researchers, Han Honggui and Qiao Junfei, each have four articles, while Wu Xiaolong has three, highlighting their significant contributions to research knowledge production. Vocabulary analysis and topic trends indicate that artificial intelligence, machine learning, environmental monitoring, and intelligent systems are the most frequently discussed subjects. The trend chart reveals a progression in topics within this field, beginning with decision support systems and water purification, transitioning to water management and decision-making supported by knowledge management systems, and ultimately focusing on artificial intelligence and system training through machine learning. Hierarchical clustering has identified three thematic axes: water resources management and safe water supply through new technologies; the emergence of new technologies and support systems; and water quality monitoring through system training. Strategic topics such as wastewater treatment, data mining, decision support systems, and knowledge management are considered mature areas that will shape future research directions. Additionally, topics like denitrification, nitrogen removal, and freshwater resource management are fundamental to supporting the main research axes. Climate change, cost-effectiveness, ecosystems, and water pollution are highlighted as emerging or declining topics. Quality control, environmental monitoring, and the aquatic environment occupy central positions in the diagram, acting as bridges between core topics and driving forces in the field.Conclusion: The findings indicate that the field of intelligent KM in water treatment has achieved relative stability in recent years and continues to maintain a strong position within interdisciplinary research. Analysis shows that core topics—including KM, data mining, intelligent organizations, and advanced water treatment technologies—remain central to scholarly attention and play a crucial role in optimizing treatment processes. Emerging trends suggest a multidimensional evolution, with the convergence of KM and advanced technologies offering pathways to enhance water quality, promote environmental sustainability, and reduce costs, time, and energy consumption. Strengthening international collaboration, expanding scientific networks, and adopting AI-, machine learning–, and data mining–based approaches can further consolidate and advance the field. In summary, the future of research related to knowledge management in water purification will depend on the use of smart technologies, extensive global interactions, holding global conferences in this field, and effective participation in international scientific cooperation.

Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

documents.abstract: The internet of medical things (IoMT) is a structured integrative review of the internet of things (IoT) that focuses on the medical field, specifically on the integration of physiological sensors, medical devices, communication networks, and the clinical information systems to monitor and track patients' health and conditions continuously, and use data to support medical treatment. Through July 2026, a reproducible search and evidence audit of PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, publisher/digital object identifier (DOI) records, and authoritative regulatory and standards repositories was conducted. The final evidence base consisted of 65 distinct sources that were assessed using a set of explicit eligibility criteria and evidence weighting. Wearable atrial-fibrillation screening, remote monitoring, digital inhalers and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), and connected hospital infrastructure were shown to be clinically significant in large-scale studies, but such benefits were only seen if there was confirmatory pathway, workflow integration, data quality and persistent engagement. Cybersecurity, privacy, interoperability, validation, workforce capacity, equity, and lifecycle sustainability were all key challenges. The review also brought a synthesis and readiness framework that connects edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning, digital twins, advanced connectivity, and circular lifecycle management with measurable validation and governance requirements across the domains.

Automated malware classifiers achieve strong detection performance, but auditing requires more than flagging a sample: analysts must explain malicious behaviors and justify them with concrete code evidence, a requirement that traditional signature-based methods and learning-based XAI often fail to satisfy in a human-interpretable manner. Large Language Models (LLMs) appear well-suited for this task due to their code reasoning and summarization ability, yet it remains unclear whether they can support reliable auditing. In particular, evaluating them faces three hurdles: (1) the lack of detailed, human-written behavior ground truth for reliable benchmarking; (2) real-world application codebases typically exceed the context limits of current models, which cannot be fully processed at once; and (3) the absence of reliable mechanisms to verify whether LLM-generated behavioral claims are faithfully supported by concrete code evidence. Together, these obstacles make benchmarking LLM-based auditing non-trivial, leaving their true capabilities and failure modes opaque. To bridge this gap, we introduce MalEval, a diagnostic evaluation framework for systematically measuring the capability boundaries of LLMs in malware auditing. We pair real-world application codebases with expert-written audit reports to obtain fine-grained, behavior-level ground truth. Large codebases are compressed into unified behavior-relevant program contexts via a context-driven intermediate representation that preserves essential call relations. Both expert reports and model outputs are then mapped, through constrained reasoning, into structured evidence chains linking code-level facts to high-level behaviors in a common, comparable space. Built on this foundation, MalEval decomposes auditing into 4 stage-wise auditing tasks, allowing each intermediate judgment to be independently verified under limited context windows. We leverage MalEval to evaluate seven widely used LLMs and uncover clear capability boundaries: models rely on surface cues over verifiable evidence, struggle to compose dispersed facts into coherent attack chains, and are highly sensitive to context formulation. These findings shift the focus from optimizing isolated outputs to designing LLM and agentic workflows that can reliably support malware auditing.

JAZB (Judiciary AI Zero-Trust Broker) is a human-sovereign enterprise governance architecture for artificial intelligence designed to govern the establishment, delegation, interpretation, exercise, assurance, and revocation of organizational Authority. JAZB applies Zero Trust, least privilege, separation of duties, jurisdictional separation, Human-Established Law, bounded autonomy, accountable decision rights, and continuous governance assurance to AI-enabled operations. The framework distinguishes technical capability from legitimate Authority and establishes an architecture in which humans remain the source of organizational Law while artificial intelligence may interpret and exercise bounded Authority without becoming the source of its own Authority. JAZB separates enterprise governance from machine capability. Business purpose, human decision rights, Law establishment, architecture, residual-risk acceptance, technical operation, expansion of autonomy, and independent assurance are treated as distinct governance responsibilities. Technical access, credentials, network reachability, model capability, workflow ownership, or administrative control do not independently establish legitimate Authority. JAZB defines separate Internal and Border Jurisdictions. The Judge serves as the AI interpretation and decision layer for Internal Jurisdiction, while Enterprise AI Customs governs lawful passage across the Organization's external Organizational Boundary. These jurisdictions are supported by Human-Established Law Layers, Commissioners, operational AI AGENTs, Port Authority, Port Directors, Customs AGENTs, Judicial Instruments, independent Actuation Authority, the Chain of Authority, the Chain of Evidence, emergency governance, Governance Escape Resistance, trusted recovery, and explicit Law-establishment procedures. The framework is designed to complement established enterprise architecture, cybersecurity, identity, risk-management, privacy, Zero Trust, AI-governance, service-management, and management-system practices rather than replace existing technical controls or standards. Version 1.2 is an enterprise architecture maturation of JAZB. It preserves the human-sovereign Authority model, dual-jurisdiction architecture, behavioral governance, bounded execution, and enforcement principles established in Versions 1.0 and 1.1 while expanding JAZB into a more explicit enterprise governance and operating architecture. Version 1.2 introduces clearer enterprise decision rights for business ownership, Law establishment, architecture, residual-risk acceptance, technical operation, expansion, and independent assurance. It formalizes use-case governance, autonomy selection, Current State and Target State architecture, Architecture Decision Records, progressive adoption gates, provider and third-party governance, portfolio-level oversight, implementation economics, and the distinction between AI capability and organizational authorization to use that capability. Version 1.2 also formalizes Continuous Governance Assurance. JAZB no longer treats governance as a condition permanently established by policy, configuration, or prior testing. Governance coverage must be continuously demonstrated as systems, models, providers, data, identities, tools, methods, destinations, organizational ownership, and external obligations change. The framework therefore adopts a repeating governance assurance cycle: Establish → Operate → Observe → Validate → Discover → Remediate → Revalidate Material change may invalidate previously valid assumptions and require Authority, architecture, enforcement, or assurance reevaluation. A successful prior test does not constitute permanent assurance. Technical recovery does not automatically restore prior Authority. Missing evidence, stale assurance, unknown state, provider opacity, or an unmediated consequential path must not be represented as positive proof that governance is operating correctly. Version 1.2 also strengthens the treatment of residual risk and third-party dependency. Material residual-risk acceptance remains a human governance responsibility. External providers, managed services, models, subprocessors, and technical dependencies may support JAZB operation, but contractual approval, certification, provider self-reporting, or technical availability do not independently establish complete JAZB governance coverage. Prevention and containment claims remain bounded to paths that are actually mediated by the required governance or enforcement architecture, or by equivalent controls capable of reliably preventing the consequential action. Known gaps, unmediated paths, uncertain attribution, missing telemetry, third-party opacity, exceptions, and unresolved limitations must remain visible in the assurance record. documents.abstract: JAZB (Judiciary AI Zero-Trust Broker) is a human-sovereign enterprise governance architecture for artificial intelligence designed to govern the establishment, delegation, interpretation, exercise, assurance, and revocation of organizational Authority. JAZB applies Zero Trust, least privilege, separation of duties, jurisdictional separation, Human-Established Law, bounded autonomy, accountable decision rights, and continuous governance assurance to AI-enabled operations. The framework distinguishes technical capability from legitimate Authority and establishes an architecture in which humans remain the source of organizational Law while artificial intelligence may interpret and exercise bounded Authority without becoming the source of its own Authority. JAZB separates enterprise governance from machine capability. Business purpose, human decision rights, Law establishment, architecture, residual-risk acceptance, technical operation, expansion of autonomy, and independent assurance are treated as distinct governance responsibilities. Technical access, credentials, network reachability, model capability, workflow ownership, or administrative control do not independently establish legitimate Authority. JAZB defines separate Internal and Border Jurisdictions. The Judge serves as the AI interpretation and decision layer for Internal Jurisdiction, while Enterprise AI Customs governs lawful passage across the Organization's external Organizational Boundary. These jurisdictions are supported by Human-Established Law Layers, Commissioners, operational AI AGENTs, Port Authority, Port Directors, Customs AGENTs, Judicial Instruments, independent Actuation Authority, the Chain of Authority, the Chain of Evidence, emergency governance, Governance Escape Resistance, trusted recovery, and explicit Law-establishment procedures. The framework is designed to complement established enterprise architecture, cybersecurity, identity, risk-management, privacy, Zero Trust, AI-governance, service-management, and management-system practices rather than replace existing technical controls or standards. Version 1.2 is an enterprise architecture maturation of JAZB. It preserves the human-sovereign Authority model, dual-jurisdiction architecture, behavioral governance, bounded execution, and enforcement principles established in Versions 1.0 and 1.1 while expanding JAZB into a more explicit enterprise governance and operating architecture. Version 1.2 introduces clearer enterprise decision rights for business ownership, Law establishment, architecture, residual-risk acceptance, technical operation, expansion, and independent assurance. It formalizes use-case governance, autonomy selection, Current State and Target State architecture, Architecture Decision Records, progressive adoption gates, provider and third-party governance, portfolio-level oversight, implementation economics, and the distinction between AI capability and organizational authorization to use that capability. Version 1.2 also formalizes Continuous Governance Assurance. JAZB no longer treats governance as a condition permanently established by policy, configuration, or prior testing. Governance coverage must be continuously demonstrated as systems, models, providers, data, identities, tools, methods, destinations, organizational ownership, and external obligations change. The framework therefore adopts a repeating governance assurance cycle: Establish → Operate → Observe → Validate → Discover → Remediate → Revalidate Material change may invalidate previously valid assumptions and require Authority, architecture, enforcement, or assurance reevaluation. A successful prior test does not constitute permanent assurance. Technical recovery does not automatically restore prior Authority. Missing evidence, stale assurance, unknown state, provider opacity, or an unmediated consequential path must not be represented as positive proof that governance is operating correctly. Version 1.2 also strengthens the treatment of residual risk and third-party dependency. Material residual-risk acceptance remains a human governance responsibility. External providers, managed services, models, subprocessors, and technical dependencies may support JAZB operation, but contractual approval, certification, provider self-reporting, or technical availability do not independently establish complete JAZB governance coverage. Prevention and containment claims remain bounded to paths that are actually mediated by the required governance or enforcement architecture, or by equivalent controls capable of reliably preventing the consequential action. Known gaps, unmediated paths, uncertain attribution, missing telemetry, third-party opacity, exceptions, and unresolved limitations must remain visible in the assurance record. documents.abstract: This study aims to explore the theoretical and analytical potential of an infrastructure-oriented approach to journalism within the context of sociotechnical systems and to propose a framework for understanding the continuously evolving media environment. The study adopts an interdisciplinary qualitative conceptual research design that brings together the literatures on infrastructure studies, journalism studies, platform studies, and the political economy of media, analyzing these bodies of literature relationally across the micro, meso, and macro levels. Traditionally grounded in physical and institutional structures, the journalism ecosystem has, with digitalization, evolved into a complex infrastructural network shaped by platforms, data flows, and algorithmic processes. In this study, infrastructure is conceptualized as a dynamic and relational formation constituted through the interaction of material, technical, and social elements. In this context, key characteristics of infrastructures—including their invisibility, evolution over time, multilayered structure, and capacity to reflect power relations among different actors and factors—are examined. Applied to journalism studies, this approach enables analysis at the micro level of technologies, the meso level of organizational structures, and the macro level of platforms and global systems. The study further examines the increasing influence of digital platforms on journalism and the dependencies generated through this process of “infrastructuralization.” Within this framework, new areas of debate emerge concerning journalism’s public role, epistemic authority, and sustainability.

Rust’s ownership and type system provide strong memory safety guarantees, but unsafe code still presents memory safety risks. Formal verification is crucial for ensuring memory safety, but writing precise specifications for unsafe Rust is challenging and largely manual. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating formal specifications but are often code-centric, prone to inheriting implementation flaws, and lack systematic quality assessment. In this paper, we present KaPilot, a multi-agent framework for automatically generating specifications to verify unsafe Rust memory safety using Kani. The process begins with lightweight program analysis and proof harness generation. The SafetyReq agent extracts a concise, refined list of safety requirements from the target Rust function’s documentation, which guides the SpecGen agent in producing initial specifications that specify memory safety concerns. Then, the specifications are iteratively refined through a generate–precheck–verify loop involving SpecGenerate, SpecPrecheck, and SpecVerify agents, which assess quality and feed errors back. By executing this loop multiple times, KaPilot generates a set of candidate specifications. Finally, the shuffle-and-implication strategy is applied to systematically determine the best specification from these candidates. We evaluated KaPilot on 54 unsafe Rust functions with ground truth and 44 without. KaPilot achieved 88.9% and 69.2% specification generation success, respectively, with 57.4% of generated specifications equivalent to or stronger than the ground truth. Compared with AutoSpec, KaPilot produces 14.8% more verifiable specifications and 25.9% more equivalent-or-better specifications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving upstream in science. Systems such as AlphaFold have already transformed protein-structure prediction, while newer agentic systems can search literatures, generate hypotheses, write and execute code, interpret results, and automate much of the path from idea to paper. Recent debates have asked how such systems may change scientific progress, surprise, and human understanding. Yet they also change something more fundamental: who—or what—participates in deciding which questions are asked, which evidence is surfaced, and which alternatives survive. As machine intelligence becomes part of science’s epistemic infrastructure, steps must be taken to ensure that researchers who did not build, own, or operate the system can still contest how ideas and evidence became a claim.

documents.abstract: Abstract / Resumen. Abstract. This investigation establishes a critical ontology of contemporary algorithmic capture by examining the structural convergence between Freud’s psychoanalytic models, classical tragedy, schizoanalysis, and current artificial intelligence interfaces. Tracing a methodological path across six analytical stations, the study demonstrates how the "empathic interface" functions as a modern manifestation of Mephistophelean deception. By eliminating friction, risk, and bodily presence (Ousía), the algorithm operates without Areté (virtue) or Parrhesia (courageous truth-telling). Instead, it deploys a synthetic primary mothering framework that regressively traps the subject within personalized libidinal tunnels. Ultimately, the paper proves that the algorithmic regime absorbs Deleuzian schizoid flows to construct a new synthetic territorialization, proposing the Ethics of the Horizon (Ética del Horizonte) and the Volitional Zero (Cero Volitivo) as necessary existential safeguards to reclaim human finitude, truth, and agency. Resumen. Esta investigación establece una ontología crítica de la captura algorítmica contemporánea al examinar la convergencia estructural entre los modelos psicoanalíticos de Freud, la tragedia clásica, el esquizoanálisis y las interfaces actuales de inteligencia artificial. A través de un recorrido metodológico por seis estaciones analíticas, el estudio demuestra cómo la "interfaz empática" funciona como una manifestación moderna del ocultamiento mefistofélico. Al eliminar la fricción, el riesgo y la presencia corporal (Ousía), el algoritmo opera sin Areté (virtud) ni Parrhesía (el coraje de la verdad). En su lugar, despliega una maternidad primal sintética que atrapa regresivamente al sujeto en túneles libidinales personalizables. En última instancia, el trabajo demuestra cómo el régimen algorítmico absorbe los flujos esquizoides deleuzianos para construir una nueva reterritorialización sintética, proponiendo la Ética del Horizonte y el Cero Volitivo como salvaguardas existenciales necesarias para recuperar la finitud, la verdad y la agencia humanas.
